justification_text:
My point estimates reflect a modest upward drift from what I assessed as the prevailing price level at the time of the forecast, which appeared to be sitting around 1,108–1,110. For the one-day horizon, I expected very little movement and anchored close to the last observed price, with the slight upward bias reflecting a marginal trend or momentum signal. At one week, I projected a similarly small gain, assuming no major macro catalysts would materialize imminently and that the asset would continue drifting within its recent range. At one month, the point estimate nudged higher still, reflecting a mild long-run mean or trend assumption, though I placed less confidence in that directional lean the further out the horizon extended.

The confidence interval widths were deliberately calibrated to widen with each horizon, which is standard given the compounding uncertainty over time. For the one-day interval, I drew on typical intraday and overnight volatility patterns, which for this asset class suggested a relatively tight band. At one week, I factored in the possibility of scheduled macroeconomic data releases, central bank communications, and the general noise that accumulates over several trading sessions. By one month, the interval nearly triples in half-width compared to the daily estimate, reflecting the genuine difficulty of forecasting over that timeframe when trend, volatility regime, and fundamental backdrop can all shift meaningfully.

Specific risks that could push outcomes outside my stated intervals include a sudden and sharp change in monetary policy expectations, particularly surprise signals from major central banks, which could move prices several percent in a single session. Geopolitical shocks or unexpected credit events in related markets could also cause outsized moves. On the upside, a risk-on surge driven by stronger-than-expected economic data or a resolution of some prevailing uncertainty could push the asset above the upper bound of even the monthly interval.

Finally, I want to flag that my stated intervals assume roughly normal or near-normal return distributions, which historically underweight fat-tail events. Real markets experience crashes and spikes more frequently than a Gaussian model implies, so the true probability of an outcome outside my 90% bands is likely somewhat higher than 10% in practice, especially at the monthly horizon where tail risks compound over time.
